Landmark trials examining supervised combined aerobic and resistance exercise programs over twelve weeks documented significant increases in total and appendicular lean mass, muscular strength, and walking capacity, accompanied by decreases in fatigue and circulating C-reactive protein levels. ### 3.4. Management of ADT-Induced Muscle Loss
The muscle loss induced by ADT primarily results from androgen withdrawal; interventions that directly stimulate skeletal muscle therefore represent the most rational counter-strategies, and among these, resistance exercise training has by far the strongest supporting evidence. Multiple randomised controlled trials have shown that supervised resistance training increases muscle mass and strength and improves physical functioning and quality of life in men receiving ADT [33,34].
In a pilot randomised trial, a substantial proportion of men beginning ADT already met mass-based criteria for sarcopenia (43.8%) or met criteria for metabolic syndrome at baseline (40.6%), and a 12-week resistance-training programme significantly improved lean mass, reduced body-fat percentage, increased strength, and enhanced prostate-cancer-specific quality of life [35].

context.title: Myosteatosis and Sarcopenic Obesity in Men Receiving Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Prostate Cancer: Rationale for Mechanism-Driven Multimodal Intervention
context.snippet: ## Simple Summary Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a cornerstone of prostate cancer treatment but is associated with significant adverse effects on body composition and metabolic health. These include loss of skeletal muscle, increased fat mass, and development of sarcopenic obesity, a condition linked to functional decline, metabolic syndrome, and potentially adverse oncologic outcomes. An important and underrecognized component of this phenotype is myosteatosis, defined as the fatty infiltration of skeletal muscle, which reflects impaired muscle quality and underlying metabolic dysfunction. This structured narrative review synthesizes current evidence on interventions aimed at mitigating sarcopenic obesity in men receiving ADT. While exercise and nutrition-based strategies have shown benefits in improving muscle strength and body composition, most studies are limited by small sample sizes, short durations, and the lack of assessment of muscle quality. Notably, myosteatosis-specific endpoints remain rarely incorporated in clinical trials of men receiving ADT. We propose a mechanism-driven framework in which ADT-induced metabolic and inflammatory changes promote myosteatosis, which in turn, contributes to sarcopenic obesity and associated clinical outcomes. Future interventions should incorporate multimodal strategies and include imaging-based measures of muscle quality to better guide clinical management and improve survivorship outcomes. Exercise is known to reduce adverse side effects of Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) on quality of life, bone health and fatigue for prostate cancer (PCa) patients. To compare the effects of exercise-based interventions on cardiometabolic health and fatigue in men with prostate cancer receiving androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13114672/)Abstract

Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a cornerstone of prostate cancer treatment but is associated with significant adverse effects on body composition and metabolic health. These include loss of skeletal muscle, increased fat mass, and development of sarcopenic obesity, a condition linked to functional decline, metabolic syndrome, and potentially adverse oncologic outcomes. An important and underrecognized component of this phenotype is myosteatosis, defined as the fatty infiltration of skeletal muscle, which reflects impaired muscle quality and underlying metabolic dysfunction. This structured narrative review synthesizes current evidence on interventions aimed at mitigating sarcopenic obesity in men receiving ADT. While exercise and nutrition-based strategies have shown benefits in improving muscle strength and body composition, most studies are limited by small sample sizes, short durations, and the lack of assessment of muscle quality. Notably, myosteatosis-specific endpoints remain rarely incorporated in clinical trials of men receiving ADT. We propose a mechanism-driven framework in which ADT-induced metabolic and inflammatory changes promote myosteatosis, which in turn, contributes to sarcopenic obesity and associated clinical outcomes. Future interventions should incorporate multimodal strategies and include imaging-based measures of muscle quality to better guide clinical management and improve survivorship outcomes.

Androgen deprivation therapy serves as a cornerstone treatment for achieving disease control and improving survival in prostate cancer, yet suppressing circulating testosterone induces clinically significant adverse consequences across the musculoskeletal and metabolic systems. In a narrative synthesis published in Supportive Care in Cancer, researchers analyzed fifteen years of published studies to evaluate how structured physical exercise and targeted nutritional regimens counteract hormone treatment side effects. The review highlights that systemic androgen suppression rapidly triggers osteosarcopenia—the concurrent loss of skeletal muscle mass, muscular strength, and bone mineral density—alongside increases in body fat that drive a sarcopenic-obesity phenotype. By examining 30 selected primary studies and systematic reviews, the authors demonstrate that integrating multimodal lifestyle programs into routine clinical oncology pathways provides substantial systemic benefits that single-modality therapies fail to achieve.

The biological mechanisms connecting testosterone suppression to tissue breakdown are complex and multidirectional. When circulating testosterone declines below 0.5 nanograms per milliliter, androgen receptor signaling becomes downregulated, directly suppressing skeletal muscle protein synthesis, impairing mitochondrial efficiency, and encouraging adipose infiltration within muscular compartments. Concurrently, diminished aromatase conversion of testosterone drives severe estradiol depletion below 20 percent of normal values. This estrogen deficit alters the balance of the RANKL and osteoprotegerin regulatory pathway across osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts, while suppressing the growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor axis. Together, these intersecting endocrine disruptions accelerate osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, causing cortical thinning, trabecular degradation, and an elevated vulnerability to falls and fragility fractures

keenable.snippet:
Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a key treatment for prostate cancer, helping to improve disease control and survival. However, reducing circulating testosterone leads to significant and clinically relevant side effects. These include a rapid decline in musculoskeletal health, marked by loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, and decreased bone mineral density. The coexistence of low muscle mass and reduced bone mineral density defines osteosarcopenia, whereas the concurrent gain in body fat reflects an associated sarcopenic-obesity phenotype rather than part of the definition itself (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00520-026-11504-1#Fig1)).

The pathophysiology of osteosarcopenia induced by ADT is complex and involves multiple factors. Testosterone deficiency leads to a catabolic environment characterized by reduced muscle protein synthesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased fat accumulation into muscle tissue (sarcopenic obesity). Concurrently, the depletion of estrogen, resulting from suppressed aromatization of testosterone, accelerates bone resorption, which contributes to cortical thinning and deterioration of trabecular bone. These changes occur rapidly, with prospective studies indicating measurable reductions in lean mass and bone density within the first 6 to 12 months after initiating ADT, alongside cumulative effects over time. Additionally, evidence points to an increase in fat mass, insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation associated with ADT, further compromising musculoskeletal integrity [7,8,[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00520-026-11504-1#ref-CR9)].

The study found that a lifestyle intervention, which included personalized exercise and dietary prescriptions, led to significant improvements in adiposity and lean mass. These interventions helped to attenuate or reverse the adverse effects of ADT, which can contribute to frailty and functional decline.

Authors: Fiorella Ambrosio, Martina Persia, Andrea Bellieni, Luca Tagliaferri, Maria Antonietta Gambacorta, Vincenzo Frascino, Gabriele Abbatecola, Francesco Landi, Giuseppe Ferdinando Colloca

Abstract

Background: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is associated with significant changes in body composition, promoting bone and muscle loss and increasing the risk of osteosarcopenia. This condition predisposes patients to adverse events such as falls, fractures, loss of functional autonomy, and increased cardiovascular risk, with possible repercussions on oncological outcomes and, in general, on patients’ quality of life.

Objectives: This narrative review explores the available evidence on the role of exercise, nutrition, and the use of drug therapies in the prevention and management of ADT-induced osteosarcopenia, identifying the future perspectives in the integrated management of patients with prostate cancer undergoing hormone treatment.

Methods: This review explores studies published over the last 15 years and aims to select scientific contributions concerning the effects of physical exercise, nutrition, or combined interventions on musculoskeletal health in subjects undergoing androgen deprivation therapy.

Results: Resistance training represents a promising non-pharmacological approach for the management of ADT-induced musculoskeletal alterations. Such programs have demonstrated efficacy in preserving lean body mass, potentially mitigating bone loss, and improving physical performance.

Abstract

Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the most effective systemic treatment for prostate cancer and can be succeeded either surgically or pharmaceutically. Both approaches lead to hypogonadism with a large variety of adverse events, including obesity, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction. However, patients receiving ADT must be well informed about the potential benefits as well as the risks of the treatment.

seltz.snippet:
## Introduction

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in two-thirds of the world, with approximately 1.5 million new cases recorded annually [1]. In the 2022 age-standardized incidence rates vary among continents being higher in Northern America (73.5 cases per 100,000 males) and Oceania (72.2 cases per 100,000 males), while lower in Asia (12.6 cases per 100,000 males) [2]. In Europe, it represents the most common male cancer, accounting for over 450,000 new cases each year (~ 23% of all male malignancies), with an average age-standardized incidence rate of 154 cases per 100,000 men. Driven by demographic aging, global cases are projected to reach nearly 2.9 million annually by 2040 [3].

Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a key treatment for prostate cancer, helping to improve disease control and survival. However, reducing circulating testosterone leads to significant and clinically relevant side effects. These include a rapid decline in musculoskeletal health, marked by loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, and decreased bone mineral density. The coexistence of low muscle mass and reduced bone mineral density defines osteosarcopenia, whereas the concurrent gain in body fat reflects an associated sarcopenic-obesity phenotype rather than part of the definition itself (Fig. 1).

seltz.snippet:
S**Reviewed by:** Sai Sree Reddy Basireddy, PharmD - Patient Access & Content Manager, CancerFaxUpdated **June 4, 2026**

## Why ADT Causes What It Causes: The Biology of Testosterone Deprivation

Testosterone has roles far beyond prostate cancer cell stimulation — it maintains bone density, supports muscle mass, regulates fat distribution, contributes to cardiovascular health, and drives libido. When ADT reduces testosterone to castrate levels, every tissue that testosterone normally supports is affected. Understanding the biology of each side effect makes the management rationale clear and motivates proactive intervention.

> Every ADT side effect is a consequence of removing something testosterone was doing — and each one has a specific pharmacological or lifestyle strategy that partially restores that function. ADT side effects are not inevitable suffering; they are a management challenge with available tools.

1. Predictability

   ### Why Side Effects Are Predictable
   Testosterone deprivation causes the same physiological changes regardless of how it is achieved — GnRH agonist, antagonist, or orchiectomy all produce the same side-effect profile at the same castrate testosterone level. What varies is the onset speed (antagonists are faster) and whether the effects are permanent (orchiectomy) or reversible (intermittent GnRH agonist therapy).

2. Early Action

   ### Why Early Intervention Matters
   Bone loss begins within the first 3–6 months of ADT and accelerates in the first year — starting calcium, vitamin D, and DEXA monitoring at ADT initiation rather than waiting for a fracture prevents the most clinically significant long-term consequence. The same principle applies to cardiovascular risk monitoring and hot flush management — proactive prevention is more effective than reactive treatment.

seltz.title: Hormone Therapy: Be FIERCE with Exercise
seltz.snippet:
Hormone therapy (also known as androgen deprivation therapy, ADT) can do a lot of good: in men with high-risk prostate cancer, for example, a two-year course of ADT can make the cancer more susceptible to radiation treatment, leading to a cure. And in men with cancer that has spread beyond the prostate, ADT by itself or combined with other treatment can keep cancer at bay for years.

But ADT can also cause health problems. It can raise your risk of metabolic syndrome, diabetes, heart attack, stroke, cognitive impairment, loss of muscle mass, fractures, balance issues, and falling.

Now here’s a question: Are these problems inevitable? And the answer is: We don’t know yet! PCF is funding research to help predict who is at higher risk. What we *do *know is that **you can fight ADT’s negative effects on your body**. With a PCF Challenge Award, a team of Harvard and Dana-Farber investigators led by Christina Dieli-Conwright, Ph.D., M.P.H., is leading a study to find out more: the FIERCE trial (Debunking the **F**railty-Sarcopen**I**a-ADT Axis in M**E**tastatic Prostate Cance**R** with Multi**C**omponent **E**xercise).

**Fierce** is what Dieli-Conwright, an expert in exercise oncology, would like you to be – and **against ADT, a major way to be fierce is with exercise**. “Debunking” is an interesting word choice for the study’s title. What kinds of things get debunked? False or exaggerated claims; in this case, the claims of what is *sure* to happen with ADT.

“The effects of exercise have been vastly understudied in men with metastatic prostate cancer,” Dieli-Conwright says, “particularly on how exercise can **help prevent frailty and sarcopenia**” (loss of muscle mass, strength, and function). It also can **help prevent metabolic syndrome**, a precursor to diabetes and heart disease, and this is terribly important for overall health and quality of life – affecting the entire body, not just the bones

seltz.title: Staying Strong and Preventing Falls
seltz.snippet:
Let’s think, for a minute, about falling – said no one ever. Nobody wants to think about falling! It’s awful! Plus, you may be thinking: “I’ve got prostate cancer! *That’s* my main concern!”

Falling *is* awful, but the thing is, **if you are on androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), in addition to fighting *against* prostate cancer, you need to fight *for* your body. ** You are at higher risk of bone thinning, loss of muscle mass and falling, in addition to some other health problems associated with weight gain and metabolic syndrome.

Falls can be injurious to anyone, but if your bones are weakened and your muscles are not strong, you can get a fracture – and this can be a big health setback. **But here’s good news**, from PCF-funded investigator Christina Dieli-Conwright, Ph.D., M.P.H., an expert in exercise oncology at Dana Farber Cancer Institute. The loss of muscle mass, strength, and function, and the gain of fat and ADT “don’t have to go hand in hand.” **Exercise can help prevent these problems.**

### **What Kind of Exercise? **

Patients on ADT need a well-rounded approach: cardiovascular exercise, strength training, stretching, and functional exercises to improve balance and movement, says Dieli-Conwright. Note: ADT takes away testosterone, and testosterone makes muscles big. ## Why Bone Health Matters

Bones are living tissue that constantly renews itself. When resorption (breakdown) outpaces formation, overall strength declines. In prostate cancer patients, fractures are more than painful inconveniences:

- They can **limit mobility**, leading to muscle weakness and weight gain.
- They **increase hospitalization risk** and complications.
- They may **delay cancer treatments** or other therapies.

Protecting your bones from the start of ADT is as important as monitoring your cancer markers.

---

## Key Protective Protocols

Below are evidence-based steps to help offset bone loss during prostate cancer treatment. Always discuss any new regimen with your healthcare team.

### 1. Regular Bone Density Testing

- DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scans measure BMD.
- Initial assessment before starting ADT establishes a baseline.
- Repeat every 12–24 months, or as your doctor recommends.

### 2. Nutrition and Supplements

Adequate intake of key nutrients supports bone remodeling:

- **Calcium**  
• Aim for 1,000–1,200 mg daily from food or supplements.  
• Dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, and canned fish with bones are top sources.
- **Vitamin D**  
• Helps calcium absorption.  
• Target 800–1,000 IU daily; your doctor may check blood levels to fine-tune dosage.
- **Protein**  
• Essential for bone matrix and muscle health.  
• Include lean meats, fish, beans, and dairy.

### 3. Weight-Bearing and Resistance Exercise

Exercise stimulates bone formation and preserves muscle mass:

- **Weight-bearing activities** (e.g., walking, stair climbing, dancing)
- **Resistance training** (e.g., free weights, resistance bands, body-weight exercises)
- **Balance and flexibility** (e.g., tai chi, yoga) reduce fall risk.

Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days. Work with a physical therapist if you’re new to structured exercise.

ultimate.title: Multimodal lifestyle strategies for ADT-induced osteosarcopenia and metabolic dysfunction in prostate cancer
ultimate.snippet:
Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a key treatment for prostate cancer, helping to improve disease control and survival. However, reducing circulating testosterone leads to significant and clinically relevant side effects. These include a rapid decline in musculoskeletal health, marked by loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, and decreased bone mineral density. The coexistence of low muscle mass and reduced bone mineral density defines osteosarcopenia, whereas the concurrent gain in body fat reflects an associated sarcopenic-obesity phenotype rather than part of the definition itself (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00520-026-11504-1#Fig1)).

The pathophysiology of osteosarcopenia induced by ADT is complex and involves multiple factors. Testosterone deficiency leads to a catabolic environment characterized by reduced muscle protein synthesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased fat accumulation into muscle tissue (sarcopenic obesity). Concurrently, the depletion of estrogen, resulting from suppressed aromatization of testosterone, accelerates bone resorption, which contributes to cortical thinning and deterioration of trabecular bone. These changes occur rapidly, with prospective studies indicating measurable reductions in lean mass and bone density within the first 6 to 12 months after initiating ADT, alongside cumulative effects over time. Additionally, evidence points to an increase in fat mass, insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation associated with ADT, further compromising musculoskeletal integrity [7,8,[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00520-026-11504-1#ref-CR9)].

The study found that a lifestyle intervention, which included personalized exercise and dietary prescriptions, led to significant improvements in adiposity and lean mass. These interventions helped to attenuate or reverse the adverse effects of ADT, which can contribute to frailty and functional decline.

ultimate.title: Lifestyle Interventions Counter Musculoskeletal and Metabolic Decline
ultimate.snippet: Combining resistance training with structured aerobic exercise creates a multimodal physical regimen that simultaneously targets cardiovascular and metabolic sequelae. Landmark trials examining supervised combined aerobic and resistance exercise programs over twelve weeks documented significant increases in total and appendicular lean mass, muscular strength, and walking capacity, accompanied by decreases in fatigue and circulating C-reactive protein levels. Aerobic exercise interventions alone improve cardiorespiratory fitness, such as peak oxygen uptake, and mitigate treatment-related fatigue, but demonstrate limited capacity to preserve skeletal muscle volume. When high-intensity interval training or progressive aerobic exercise is added to resistance protocols, patients achieve broader systemic adaptations, including reductions in visceral adiposity, improved glycemic metrics, and lower resting diastolic blood pressure.

ultimate.title: Myosteatosis and Sarcopenic Obesity in Men Receiving Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Prostate Cancer: Rationale for Mechanism-Driven Multimodal Intervention
ultimate.snippet:
The hormonal shifts associated with ADT induce substantial changes in body composition and metabolism, including increased fat mass, reduced lean body mass, altered lipid profiles, hyperglycemia, decreased insulin sensitivity, osteoporosis, and metabolic syndrome [5,6,7,8,9,10]. These changes may culminate in a clinical phenotype consistent with sarcopenic obesity (SO), characterized by the coexistence of sarcopenia and excess adiposity [6,7,11,12,13]. ADT-induced testosterone depletion contributes to reduced muscle protein synthesis and increased muscle catabolism, while also promoting visceral adiposity and metabolic dysfunction [5,7,8,9].

We therefore propose that myosteatosis should be considered a key biomarker of ADT-induced sarcopenic obesity [15], linking metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and skeletal muscle deterioration in this population.

Based on current evidence, future interventions designed to mitigate SO and associated metabolic abnormalities in men receiving ADT should evaluate comprehensive, bundled, evidence-based strategies initiated early in the course of treatment, ideally within 3 months of starting ADT. These bundled interventions should include: (a) a nutrition plan emphasizing low-glycemic, minimally processed foods, high intake of plant-based phytochemical-rich foods, and adequate protein intake; (b) omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and appropriate micronutrient support, including vitamin D and calcium when indicated; (c) structured aerobic exercise; (d) progressive resistance training; and (e) carefully monitored time-restricted eating or related metabolic timing strategies when feasible and safe.

ultimate.title: **Musculoskeletal and metabolic effects of androgen deprivation therapy in men with prostate cancer**
ultimate.snippet:
The aim of this review is to summarize contemporary evidence on the impact of androgen deficiency and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer on muscle-bone and cardiometabolic health in men. The key physiological mechanisms by which testosterone, including its aromatisation to estradiol, regulates bone remodelling, muscle-bone crosstalk, and the maintenance of skeletal integrity are outlined. We also discuss studies demonstrating the relationships between low testosterone and estradiol concentrations, elevated sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels, reduced bone mineral density (BMD), and an increased risk of osteoporotic fractures in men.
The effects of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) on BMD and muscle mass are reviewed, with emphasis on the fact that, despite consistent improvements in skeletal parameters, current data do not allow firm conclusions to be drawn regarding fracture risk reduction. Particular attention is paid to the metabolic and inflammatory sequelae of ADT—including dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation and increased cardiovascular risk—and their links with sarcopenia and osteosarcopenia.
Finally, we discuss clinical strategies for early identification and risk stratification, including DXA screening, assessment of muscle strength and cardiometabolic profile, and a multidisciplinary approach that combines antiresorptive therapy, lifestyle optimization, and structured exercise programmes to mitigate the adverse effects of ADT. The need for an individualised approach in men with hypogonadism, especially those receiving ADT, is highlighted, as is the need for future studies evaluating combined pharmacological and non-pharmacological preventive strategies, including novel osteoanabolic agents and targeted therapies for sarcopenia.

Lifestyle Modification and Physical Exercise
The cessation of smoking, moderate sun exposure, and limited alcohol intake of less than two standard drinks (one standard drink contains 14 g or 0.6 fluid ounces of pure alcohol) per day are non-pharmacological interventions that can be recommended to patients on ADT [63,65]. Sarcopenia is a degenerative loss of muscle mass closely associated with physical frailty, which increases the risk of falls and subsequent risk of skeletal fractures [83]. When sarcopenic patients are exposed to ADT, the risk of fracture increases along with its potentially life-threatening complications [84]. Countermeasures for ADT-induced sarcopenia should include muscle-strengthening exercise and evaluation for fall prevention. Such evaluations include neurological examination and a thorough assessment of prescription medications for side effects that could affect balance [85]. ultimate.snippet: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in men with prostate cancer increases the risk of osteoporotic fractures, type 2 diabetes and, possibly, cardiovascular events. There is considerable uncertainty about the risk-benefit ratio of ADT in non-palliative treatment; the benefits of ADT in treating non-metastatic prostate cancer need to be carefully weighed against the risks of ADT-induced adverse events. Baseline assessment of bone health at the initiation of ADT should include measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry and, in men with osteopaenia, a thoracolumbar spine x-ray. General measures to prevent bone loss, including regular physical activity, as well as ensuring calcium and vitamin D sufficiency, should be instituted routinely. All men with a previous minimal trauma fracture should receive pharmacological therapy unless contraindicated; for those who have not sustained a minimal trauma fracture, treatment is advised if the BMD T score is ≤ - 2.0, or if the 10-year risk of a major osteoporotic fracture exceeds 20%. Men with prostate cancer who are receiving ADT should be closely monitored for weight gain and diabetes; intensive lifestyle intervention is recommended to prevent ADT-induced weight gain and insulin resistance. Management of the metabolic sequelae of ADT includes optimal reduction of cardiovascular risk factors, with particular attention to weight, blood pressure, lipid profile, smoking cessation, and glycaemic control.
